tip: The verb marks the subject's gender too: वह जाती है (vah jaati hai = she goes) has -ती because she's female; a boy would be जाता है (jaata hai).
'Wear' depends on the item: हेडफ़ोन लगाकर (headphone lagaakar) uses लगाना (lagaana = attach); clothes take पहनना (pahenna). Each item picks its verb.
ठीक (theek) usually means 'fine, okay' – but before a time it means sharp: ठीक छह बजे (theek chhah baje) = at exactly six.
Going somewhere to do something uses the -ने (-ne) verb form: टहलने जाते हैं (tahalne jaate hain) = go for a stroll, literally 'go to stroll'. No 'for' needed.
Hindi has no '-est'. सबसे पहले (sabse pehle) = first of all, literally 'than all, earlier'. सबसे (sabse) + any quality word means 'the most'.
से (se) means 'from' – and also 'by': बस से (bas se) = by bus. Every means of transport takes से; context tells you which sense is meant.
In an 'X और Y' list, दोनों (donon = both) comes at the end: योग और ध्यान दोनों (yog aur dhyaan donon) = both yoga and meditation.
One vowel makes it 'make someone laugh': हँसना (hansna = laugh) → हँसाता (hansaata = makes laugh). No extra 'make' verb – the -आ- (-aa-) does it.
Skills 'come to you': खाना बनाना आता है (khaana banaana aata hai) = literally 'does making food come to you'. Knowing how = the skill + आना (aana = come).
ननिहाल (nanihaal) is one word for 'mother's parents' home' – a classic summer-holiday destination. Hindi has exact words for each side of the family.
रहती (rahti) after another verb means 'keeps on': घूमती रहती है (ghoomti rahti hai) = keeps wandering. रहना (rahna = stay) makes an action ongoing.
सो जाता हूँ (so jaata hoon) = literally 'I go off to sleep'. Adding जाना (jaana = go) marks the change as complete – सोना (sona) alone is just 'sleep'.
'After' comes after: खाने के तुरंत बाद (khaane ke turant baad) = literally 'of eating immediately after'. Time words like बाद (baad) follow their noun.
However long the sentence, the verb normally comes last: time, place and object all pile up before साथ देते हैं (saath dete hain = stand by), which waits at the end.
कम से कम (kam se kam) = at least, literally 'less than less'. Hindi builds it by comparing कम (kam = less) with itself.
देर से आती है (der se aati hai) = comes late, literally 'comes with delay'. देर (der) is a noun – Hindi says 'with delay' where English says 'late'.
Hindi has no 'the' or 'a' – सब्ज़ी मंडी बंद है (sabzi mandi band hai) is just 'vegetable market closed is'. Context alone tells you which market.
होते हैं (hote hain) marks a general truth: ज़रूरी होते हैं (zaroori hote hain = are, as a rule, necessary). Plain हैं (hain) would pin it to right now.
English says 'has been raining'; Hindi keeps plain 'is raining': बारिश हो रही है (baarish ho rahi hai = rain is happening) + सुबह से (subah se = since morning).
क्या (kya) up front is a spoken question mark: क्या यह सच है (kya yeh sach hai) = is this true? Without it, यह सच है (yeh sach hai) states 'this is true'.
Things 'come into' a space when they fit: ज़्यादा सामान नहीं आता (zyaada saamaan nahin aata = more stuff doesn't come) = no more fits. Rooms, boxes, clothes all work this way.
-कर (-kar) glued to a verb means 'after doing it': उठकर (uthkar = having gotten up). One ending does the work of English 'after waking up'.
के लिए (ke liye = for) comes after its noun, not before: बुखार के लिए (bukhaar ke liye = fever for). Hindi's little linking words all trail the noun.
मुझे ... करना है (mujhe ... karna hai) is literally 'to me it is to-do' – Hindi's 'I have to'. फ़ोन करना है (phone karna hai) = I have to make a call.
Liking lands on you in Hindi – मुझे पसंद है (mujhe pasand hai) is literally 'to me it is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे, never मैं.
In the past, a verb with an object takes ने (ne) after the subject: ग्वाले ने दूध डाला (gwaale ne doodh daala = the milkman poured milk). डाला agrees with the object दूध, not ग्वाले.
भी (bhi) normally means 'also', but next to नहीं (nahin) it means 'at all': बिलकुल भी अच्छा नहीं (bilkul bhi achha nahin) = not good at all.
The battery 'became finished': ख़त्म हो गई है (khatm ho gayi hai). Hindi frames new states as becoming – phones die, tanks fill, trains run late by 'becoming'.
You don't spend a childhood in Hindi – it passes on its own: बीता था (beeta tha = passed). बचपन (bachpan = childhood) is the subject; the village is just where it happened.
Liking lands on you: तुम्हें (tumhein = to you) plus अच्छा लगता है (achha lagta hai = strikes as good) = you like it. The person liking is the target, not the doer.
